title.en: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 Beyond Search: Zero-Shot Labels and Semantic Dedup

description.en: You've used embeddings for search — now use the same 384-dim vectors to classify text with zero training examples and to collapse near-duplicate documents before they pollute a RAG index.

story_variants.en:
## The Same 384 Numbers, Four Different Jobs

"Last time you used **all-MiniLM-L6-v2** to build search," Vaathiyaar says. "Today, a secret that saves teams from training entire models: once text lives in a good vector space, *search is just one of the things you can do there*. Classification with zero training examples. Duplicate detection with no rules. Clustering with no labels. Same model, same 80 MB, same laptop CPU — different geometry tricks."

### One Space, Many Tricks

| Job | What you compare | Training data needed |
|---|---|---|
| Semantic search | query vs. documents | none |
| Zero-shot classification | text vs. *label descriptions* | none |
| Deduplication | document vs. document | none |
| Clustering | everything vs. everything | none |

The pattern never changes: encode with `normalize_embeddings=True`, then compare with a dot product. On normalized vectors, dot product *equals* cosine similarity — one multiply-add per dimension, 384 of them, microseconds on a CPU.

### Classification Without a Dataset

A classic ML classifier needs labeled examples. An embedding classifier needs only the *names* of your classes — because label text is text too:

```python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

labels = ["billing question", "bug report", "feature request"]
label_vecs = model.encode(labels, normalize_embeddings=True)

ticket = "The app crashes every time I upload a photo"
t_vec = model.encode(ticket, normalize_embeddings=True)

scores = label_vecs @ t_vec        # one cosine score per label
print(labels[scores.argmax()])     # bug report
```

No fine-tuning, no dataset, and adding a fourth category is one string. It won't beat a trained classifier on a hard domain, but for routing support tickets, tagging notes, or triaging feedback it is shockingly strong for zero effort.

### Dedup: The Unsung Hero of Good RAG

Real document collections are full of near-duplicates — the same paragraph pasted into three wiki pages, two versions of the same FAQ. Index them all and your retriever returns the same fact five times, wasting your precious context window on redundancy. The fix is greedy semantic dedup:

1. Walk documents in order.
2. Keep a document only if its similarity to **every already-kept** document is below a threshold (0.9 works well for MiniLM).
3. Otherwise drop it — it says nothing new.

This is exactly what a local RAG assistant should do before indexing your notes: MiniLM embeds every chunk on CPU, near-twins get collapsed, and retrieval quality jumps for free. Both tricks — nearest-label and greedy dedup — are the two functions you'll implement today, in pure Python, so the geometry is never a black box.

> **Key Insight:** An embedding model isn't a search engine — it's a coordinate system for meaning. Search, zero-shot classification, dedup, and clustering are all the *same* operation — nearest neighbors by cosine — pointed at different pairs of things. Master the geometry once, and every new "AI feature" becomes a for-loop over dot products.

instruction.en: Build a zero-shot classifier with pure Python. Write `classify(vec, label_vecs)` where `vec` is a normalized embedding (list of floats) and `label_vecs` is a dict mapping label names to normalized embeddings. Return the name of the label whose dot product with `vec` is highest — that's the nearest label in the vector space. Print `classify([0.8, 0.6], {"positive": [1.0, 0.0], "negative": [-1.0, 0.0], "neutral": [0.0, 1.0]})`.

practice_challenges.starter_code:
def classify(vec: list, label_vecs: dict) -> str:
    """Return the label whose embedding is most similar to vec.
    All vectors are normalized, so dot product == cosine similarity."""
    # 1. dot product of two vectors: sum(x * y for x, y in zip(u, v))
    # 2. score every label in label_vecs against vec
    # 3. return the label name with the highest score
    pass

labels = {"positive": [1.0, 0.0], "negative": [-1.0, 0.0], "neutral": [0.0, 1.0]}
print(classify([0.8, 0.6], labels))

en: Write a helper first: def dot(u, v): return sum(x * y for x, y in zip(u, v))
max() with a key does the whole search: max(label_vecs, key=...) iterates over the label NAMES
max(label_vecs, key=lambda name: dot(vec, label_vecs[name])) returns the best name directly

practice_challenges.test_code:
labels = {"positive": [1.0, 0.0], "negative": [-1.0, 0.0], "neutral": [0.0, 1.0]}
assert classify([0.8, 0.6], labels) == "positive", f"[0.8, 0.6] points mostly along positive: got {classify([0.8, 0.6], labels)}"
assert classify([-0.6, 0.8], labels) == "neutral", f"neutral (0.8) beats negative (0.6) here: got {classify([-0.6, 0.8], labels)}"
assert classify([-0.9, -0.1], labels) == "negative", f"expected negative: got {classify([-0.9, -0.1], labels)}"
assert classify([0.6, 0.8], labels) == "neutral", "the HIGHEST dot product must win, not the first positive one"
print("All tests passed!")

instruction.en: Implement greedy semantic dedup — the preprocessing step that keeps near-duplicate chunks out of a RAG index. Write `dedup(vecs, threshold)` where `vecs` is a list of normalized embeddings. Walk the vectors in order and keep index `i` only if the dot product between `vecs[i]` and EVERY already-kept vector is below `threshold`; otherwise drop it as a near-duplicate. Return the list of kept indices. Print `dedup([[1.0, 0.0], [0.96, 0.28], [0.0, 1.0], [0.28, 0.96]], 0.9)` — vectors 1 and 3 are near-twins of earlier ones and must be dropped.

practice_challenges.starter_code:
def dedup(vecs: list, threshold: float) -> list:
    """Greedy dedup: keep a vector only if it is not too similar
    to anything already kept. Returns the kept indices."""
    # 1. kept = []  (indices of survivors)
    # 2. for each index i, vector v in enumerate(vecs):
    #      compare v against vecs[k] for every k in kept
    #      if ALL similarities are below threshold, keep i
    # 3. return kept
    pass

print(dedup([[1.0, 0.0], [0.96, 0.28], [0.0, 1.0], [0.28, 0.96]], 0.9))

en: Reuse the dot helper: def dot(u, v): return sum(x * y for x, y in zip(u, v))
all(dot(v, vecs[k]) < threshold for k in kept) is True when v is far from every survivor — and True for the first vector, since kept is empty
Append the INDEX i to kept, not the vector itself

practice_challenges.test_code:
assert dedup([[1.0, 0.0], [0.96, 0.28], [0.0, 1.0], [0.28, 0.96]], 0.9) == [0, 2], f"near-twins at 1 and 3 must be dropped: {dedup([[1.0, 0.0], [0.96, 0.28], [0.0, 1.0], [0.28, 0.96]], 0.9)}"
assert dedup([[1.0, 0.0], [0.96, 0.28], [0.0, 1.0], [0.28, 0.96]], 1.01) == [0, 1, 2, 3], "a threshold above 1.0 keeps everything"
assert dedup([[1.0, 0.0], [1.0, 0.0], [1.0, 0.0]], 0.99) == [0], "exact duplicates collapse to the first copy"
assert dedup([[0.6, 0.8]], 0.5) == [0], "a single vector is always kept"
assert dedup([[0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 0.0], [0.28, 0.96]], 0.9) == [0, 1], "compare against ALL kept vectors, not just the previous one"
print("All tests passed!")

q.en: A dedup loop keeps vecs[i] only if dot(vecs[i], vecs[i-1]) < threshold. What is the mistake?
q.ta: ஒரு dedup loop, dot(vecs[i], vecs[i-1]) < threshold என்றால் மட்டுமே vecs[i]-ஐ வைத்துக்கொள்கிறது. இதில் உள்ள தவறு என்ன?

en: The threshold must always be exactly 1.0
Dot product can't be used on normalized vectors
It should keep vectors whose similarity is above threshold
It must compare with every already-kept vector, not just the previous

under_the_hood.summary: Once texts are all-MiniLM-L6-v2 vectors, other tasks become geometry: zero-shot classification assigns the label whose description vector is most similar, and deduplication flags pairs whose cosine similarity is above a threshold.

steps.title: One space, many jobs
steps.body: Every text is a 384-d unit vector in the same space. Search compares a query with documents; classification compares a text with label descriptions; deduplication compares documents with each other. Same model, different comparisons.

steps.title: Zero-shot labels
steps.body: Write each label as a short description, such as 'a billing or payment problem' and 'a login or password problem', and embed them. For each ticket, the label with the highest cosine wins. No training examples are needed.

steps.title: Semantic deduplication
steps.body: Compute the similarity matrix of all documents with one matrix product (N x 384 times 384 x N). Pairs above a threshold such as 0.9 are near-duplicates even when the wording differs.

output: sims = vecs @ vecs.T          # N x N, diagonal = 1.0
-> ('How do I reset my password?', 'Forgot password, how to reset?')

steps.title: Thresholds need calibration
steps.body: Cosine values are not probabilities, and their typical range depends on the model and domain. Pick thresholds by checking a few dozen labelled pairs, and add a 'no label' outcome when the best score is low.

steps.title: Clustering without labels
steps.body: Feed the vectors to k-means or a density-based clusterer and topics fall out as groups. Inspect a few members of each cluster to name it.

under_the_hood.takeaway: Good embeddings turn many NLP tasks into nearest-neighbour questions. Describe labels in words, choose thresholds from data, and no training is required.
